config.title: Build command palette with fuzzy search

intro.title: Build command palette with fuzzy search
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a command palette—a searchable interface that lets users quickly find and execute commands. You'll learn how to implement fuzzy search, a technique that matches user input even with typos or missing characters. The core programming concepts involve handling user input, filtering an array of commands, and dynamically updating the UI. You'll use JavaScript fundamentals like event listeners, array methods, and string manipulation to create this interactive feature.
intro.usecase: Command palettes with fuzzy search are essential productivity tools in modern applications, allowing users to quickly access features without navigating complex menus. You'll find them in code editors like VS Code's Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), where developers can search for commands, settings, and file operations using partial or misspelled queries. This pattern also appears in design tools like Figma, productivity apps like Notion, and dashboards like GitHub's issue search, enabling efficient navigation through hundreds of options. As a developer, implementing this component teaches you how to create intuitive search interfaces that enhance user experience in data-rich applications.

objectives: Initialize and manage the state for a search query and results list
Implement a function to filter a dataset based on user input
Construct a user interface with input and results display elements
Bind event handlers to capture and respond to user keystrokes
Render dynamic search results that update in real-time
Configure the application to handle empty or no-match search states
Integrate all components to create a functional command palette

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main CommandPalette component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named CommandPalette that returns an empty fragment for now.
steps.hint: Define a function called CommandPalette that returns an empty fragment using <> and </>.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the CommandPalette component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named CommandPalette is defined and returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: The component is named CommandPalette and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named exactly 'CommandPalette' and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component is not defined correctly. Check the name and the return statement.

steps.title: Initialize state for search query
steps.instruction: Inside the CommandPalette component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'query' and initialize it to an empty string.
steps.hint: Call useState with an empty string as the initial value, and destructure the returned array into two variables: one for the current state value and one for the setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a state variable for user input
const [inputValue, setInputValue] = useState('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'query' that can store the current search input value, starting as an empty string.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with an empty string, and the returned array is destructured into 'query' and 'setQuery' variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with an empty string and destructuring the result into two variables (like [query, setQuery]).
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization isn't quite right. Remember to use the useState hook with an empty string as the initial value, and destructure the returned array.

steps.title: Define the commands data array
steps.instruction: Inside your CommandPalette component, create a constant array named 'commands' containing at least three objects. Each object should have 'id', 'name', and 'description' properties with string values representing different commands.
steps.hint: Place the array inside the component function body, before the return statement. Use the array literal syntax with square brackets, and include objects with the required properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a 'commands' array with at least three command objects, each containing id, name, and description properties.
successCriteria: The 'commands' array is defined inside the component with at least three objects, each having 'id', 'name', and 'description' string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your 'commands' array contains at least three objects, each with 'id', 'name', and 'description' properties as strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: The 'commands' array isn't properly defined. It should be a constant array containing objects with id, name, and description properties.

steps.title: Create a basic fuzzy search helper function
steps.instruction: Inside your CommandPalette component, define a function named 'fuzzyMatch' that takes two parameters: 'query' and 'string'. The function should return true if all characters in the query appear in order within the string, ignoring case differences.
steps.hint: You can create the function using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Use 'toLowerCase()' on both strings to make the comparison case-insensitive.
steps.expectedOutcome: A fuzzyMatch function is defined inside the component, ready to be used for filtering commands based on the search query.
successCriteria: The fuzzyMatch function is defined with two parameters (query, string) and implements basic case-insensitive fuzzy matching logic.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes two parameters (query and string) and returns a boolean based on whether all query characters appear in order in the string, ignoring case.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fuzzyMatch function isn't defined correctly. It should take two string parameters and return true/false based on whether all query characters appear in order in the target string (case-insensitive).

steps.title: Filter commands based on the search query
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a variable named 'filteredCommands' that filters the 'commands' array using the 'fuzzyMatch' function with the current 'query' value.
steps.hint: Use the array's filter method and call fuzzyMatch for each command. The fuzzyMatch function should check if the command's name or description matches the query.
steps.analogousExample:
// Filter an array based on a condition
const filteredItems = items.filter(item => item.includes(searchTerm));
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a filteredCommands variable that contains only the commands matching the current search query.
successCriteria: A variable named filteredCommands is declared and assigned the result of filtering the commands array using the fuzzyMatch function with the current query.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the filter method on the commands array and calling fuzzyMatch with the query for each command.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to create a filteredCommands variable that filters the commands array using the fuzzyMatch function with the current query.

steps.title: Add the main container and search input
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, replace the current `return null;` with a JSX fragment (`<>...</>`) containing a main `<div>` container with a CSS class 'command-palette' and inside it, add an `<input>` element with type 'text', placeholder 'Search commands...', and value bound to the `query` state variable.
steps.hint: The input should be controlled by the `query` state, so set its value to `query` and add an onChange handler that updates the state with the input's current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now renders a visible UI with a container div and a search input field that displays the current query value.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a JSX fragment with a div element having class 'command-palette' and an input element with type 'text', placeholder 'Search commands...', value={query}, and onChange handler that calls setQuery with e.target.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the input has all required attributes: type='text', placeholder='Search commands...', value={query}, and onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}. Also ensure the container div has the correct class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component still returns null or the structure is missing. Remember to replace `return null;` with JSX that includes a div container and an input element with the specified attributes.

steps.title: Wire the input to update search query state
steps.instruction: Inside the CommandPalette component, add value and onChange props to the search input element to connect it to the query state.
steps.hint: Set the input's value to the query state variable and update the state when the user types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The search input will now display the current query value and update it when the user types.
successCriteria: The input element has value={query} and onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both value and onChange props are correctly set on the input element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input isn't properly connected to state. Check that you've added both value={query} and onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} to the input.

steps.title: Display the filtered command results
steps.instruction: Below the input element, add a <ul> element that maps over the filteredCommands array to render each command as an <li> with its name and description.
steps.hint: Use the map method on filteredCommands to generate list items. Each list item should display the command's name and description.
steps.expectedOutcome: A list of commands appears below the search input, showing only those that match the current search query.
successCriteria: A <ul> element is added inside the command-palette div, containing <li> elements generated by mapping over filteredCommands, each displaying the command's name and description.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a list, but make sure you're mapping over filteredCommands and displaying both name and description.
steps.feedbackWrong: The list of filtered commands is not displayed correctly. Check that you've added a <ul> element with map over filteredCommands.

steps.title: Add conditional message for no results
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add conditional rendering after the input. If filteredCommands is empty, display a paragraph with the text 'No commands found'. Otherwise, render the list of filtered commands.
steps.hint: You can use a ternary operator or logical && to conditionally render content based on filteredCommands.length.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a 'No commands found' message when the search returns zero results, and show the command list when there are matches.
successCriteria: The component conditionally renders a 'No commands found' message when filteredCommands is empty, and renders the command list when it has items.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're checking filteredCommands.length and rendering the appropriate content for both empty and non-empty states.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering isn't quite right. Check that you're using filteredCommands to determine whether to show the 'No commands found' message or the command list.

steps.title: Style the command items with basic CSS
steps.instruction: Add inline styles to the li elements inside your filteredCommands map to give them padding, margin, border, and background color so they look like cards.
steps.hint: Use the style attribute with an object containing CSS properties like padding, margin, border, and backgroundColor.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: styling a list item
  • Item content
steps.expectedOutcome: The command items will have visual styling with padding, margins, borders, and a background color, making them look like distinct cards.
successCriteria: Each li element has inline styles with padding, margin, border, and backgroundColor properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure each li has padding, margin, border, and backgroundColor properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The li elements don't have the required inline styles. Add style={{ ... }} with padding, margin, border, and backgroundColor.

steps.title: Add keyboard navigation to select commands
steps.instruction: Add a new state variable called 'selectedIndex' to track which command is currently selected via keyboard navigation.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook to create a state variable that starts at -1 (meaning no selection).
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding state for selection
const [selectedIndex, setSelectedIndex] = useState(-1);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a new state variable 'selectedIndex' initialized to -1.
successCriteria: A state variable named 'selectedIndex' is declared using useState with an initial value of -1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with the correct initial value (-1).
steps.feedbackWrong: Add a state variable called 'selectedIndex' initialized to -1 using the useState hook.
